query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In a single‐phase high-entropy alloy, service or deformation conditions that provide sufficient thermomechanical energy induce local compositional segregation at high‐strain dislocation interfaces. This segregation promotes the nucleation of nanoscale, brittle intermetallic (or solute‐rich) precipitates that act as preferred crack initiation sites, thus degrading toughness even though the overall alloy remains compositionally complex.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous, single-phase, compositionally complex high-entropy alloy (e.g. an FCC HEA) with no pre-existing brittle precipitates.
generation.intervention: Apply controlled thermomechanical loading (e.g., a combination of elevated temperature cycling or slower strain rates with high plastic strain) to promote thermally assisted diffusion and local segregation.
generation.conditions: Service conditions involving sustained mechanical stress and/or moderate thermal activation that allow limited local diffusion but not full-scale phase separation across the bulk alloy.
generation.structural_mediator: Localized compositional fluctuations at dislocation walls and strain-induced nano-interfaces leading to the formation of brittle, nanoscale precipitates (e.g., Cu-rich or other solute-enriched phases) within the ductile matrix.
generation.mechanism: Under high local strain, dislocation activity creates highly distorted regions which act as sinks for solute atoms. The resulting local compositional fluctuations drive a spinodal-like decomposition or precipitation process that forms brittle intermetallic phases at nanoscale. These precipitates concentrate along deformation paths and serve as stress concentrators, thereby reducing the energy needed for crack initiation and propagation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the initial homogeneous state, loaded samples will display localized nano-precipitates at dislocation interfaces, an increase in local hardness, and a measurable drop in fracture toughness. The onset of brittle failure will correlate with the density and size of these precipitates.
generation.baseline: The as-cast or minimally deformed HEA with a homogeneous microstructure exhibiting high toughness and ductility.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be active only under conditions where the temperature and strain rate allow for some diffusion-driven segregation. Extremely low temperatures (with negligible diffusion) or conditions that favor extremely rapid deformation (limiting the time for segregation) may not trigger the brittle behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The exact threshold of strain, temperature, and dwell time needed to initiate significant segregation is uncertain, as is the specific elemental contribution (e.g. influence of Cu or other elements) to the nucleation of brittle phases.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical single-phase HEA samples. Subject one set to thermomechanical loading designed to promote local diffusion (moderate temperature with controlled strain and hold times) and the other set to a deformation protocol with rapid strain rates and minimal thermal exposure. Use high-resolution TEM, EDS mapping, and in situ mechanical testing to compare microstructural evolution, particularly the emergence of nanoscale brittle precipitates. Fracture toughness and hardness measurements should be concurrently acquired.
measurements: High-resolution TEM imaging to identify nano-scale precipitates and segregation zones.
EDS or atom probe tomography to map local compositional variations along dislocation interfaces.
Mechanical testing (tensile and fracture toughness) to compare ductility and toughness between samples.
Hardness mapping to detect localized increases in hardness associated with precipitate formation.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, under thermomechanical conditions that are predicted to promote segregation, no localized formation of brittle precipitates is observed and the fracture toughness remains comparable to the homogeneous baseline, then the mechanistic link between local segregation and brittle behavior is refuted.

Role of Cu in Nanostructural Relationship Between Phase Separation and Deformation-Induced Twinning in Heavily Drawn Non-Equiatomic High-Entropy Alloy Wire

Abstract: This study investigates the influence of Cu addition on the nanostructural evolution and mechanical performance of a heavily drawn non-equiatomic CoCu1.71FeMnNi high-entropy alloy (HEA) wire. Through systematic microstructural and compositional analysis, we examine how Cu constituent affects phase separation behavior and promotes deformation-induced nano-twinning in another phase counterpart. The designed HEA wire exhibits an elongated ultrafine dual face-centered cubic (fcc) lamella structure (i.e., Co-Fe-rich and Cu-rich phases) that emerges through compositional segregation by spontaneous phase separation from the as-cast state. High-resolution electron microscopy reveals the dislocation wall boundaries stabilized by nanoscale phase interfaces. The cold-drawn CoCu1.71FeMnNi wire features an impressive combination of strength and ductility, as well as an ultimate tensile strength of nearly ~2 GPa with an elongation of over ~6%.
